utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to all. May we begin in the usual manner by taking the day's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: For the Office of the Prosecutor, Gerard Dobbyn with Joanna Korner and our case manager Crispian Smith. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, our aides and assistants Mr. Ivan Todorovski and Dominic Kennedy appearing for Stanisic Defence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may recall that yesterday afternoon a discussion arose about the extent to which the Defence were entitled to introduce evidence relating to Crisis Staffs that had been formed by the SDA, the Croats and other such bodies, and during the adjournment, as I informed Your Honours, Mr. Zecevic and I had a discussion, and we hoped that possibly we might be able to assist Mr. Zecevic as far as the Prosecution is concerned if given a little time. Your Honours, we've been given that time, and can I immediately say what the Prosecution is prepared to state in respect of the formation of Crisis Staffs, which is as this: It is accepted by the Prosecution that all three nationalist parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA, formed Crisis Staffs. It is also accepted that Crisis Staffs could be formed for legitimate purposes. Whether in this case, Your Honours, the SDS Crisis Staffs were in fact intended to contribute to the joint criminal enterprise which is alleged in this indictment is a matter of evidence. But, for example, it is our position that facts about the Croats in Herceg-Bosna forming Crisis Staffs and using them in the commission of crimes is irrelevant to the issues in this case. So, Your Honours, I hope that makes for the purpose of the Defence the position absolutely clear. It is our position that introducing documents to show that in Herceg-Bosnia Crisis Staffs were formed is not and cannot be relevant in this case. Apart from anything else, Your Honours are in no position, and we're not trying the whole of the conflict in Herceg-Bosnia, to assess either the relevance or the weight that should be attached to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, having regard to the concession, for want of a better word, of the Prosecution of the existence of Crisis Staffs in among other ethnic groups as a fact, what is the -- could you assist us, before we definitively rule, as to where you are seeking -- what sort of foundation you're setting up having regard to your response to Mr. Dobbyn yesterday that you're not in fact advancing a tu quoque defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position of the Defence is the following: We -- we don't accept that the -- that the facts about the Crisis Staffs existing in other parts of Bosnia under the control are Muslim or Croat forces and parties is -- is not relevant to this case. We -- I'm speaking in light of the -- of the conclusions of this particular expert, because we understand the conclusions of this particular expert to be that the SDS invented these Crisis Staffs, which are illegitimate organs, that they were invented, that they were formed by the SDS for the sole purpose of furthering the joint criminal enterprise. We say, and now the Prosecution agreed to that, that it was formed everywhere, that there was nothing criminal in forming the Crisis Staffs, because those are the structures that existed in the law of the former Yugoslavia. So when -- when the situation -- the extraordinary situation developed in the former Yugoslavia in 1991, 1992, all parties went for the concept that was there already, that was known to them, and that is the concept of these committees for All People's Defence. Of course they didn't -- they didn't call it the committee, because they wouldn't go for the Communist -- for the Communist reference. They called them the Crisis Staff. Practically as the witness confirmed, they were identical. Now, this -- in our position, the -- this allegation from the Prosecution is a stronghold, one of the strongholds of their position of existence of the joint criminal enterprise, and we think that -- that it is very relevant that we show that none of that is -- is substantiated, that it's founded. Now, what we're trying to do is -- is actually put our case to the witness, which we are obliged at the very end -- in accordance with the Rule 90, and that is what -- what we are seeking to do in this -- in this case. I understand the concerns of the Trial Chamber, and the only alternative I was thinking about or compromise that we could, I don't know, propose to the Trial Chamber is that we take the very same approach as we did with Mr. Djeric. When Your Honours instructed the -- our colleagues from the Prosecution to group the documents in certain groups and then lead the evidence on only a couple of these documents and the rest with the good explanation, with the explanation in motion why does the party think is relevant can be admitted in the evidence. We are ready to proceed in -- in that respect if it pleases Your Honours, and that would save enormous amount of time and documents which we will need to present to the witness. I hope I was of assistance, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Can I just respond to that? Mr. Zecevic asked me this earlier and I said, no, I didn't object, but we do object, if Mr. Zecevic in this way wants to put in documents which relate to the Crisis Staffs run by -- no to, that we object, because we say that's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Crisis Staffs run by?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Croats or Muslims or whatever. Your Honours, we say that is not relevant, cannot be relevant, for the simple reason that in any event, it is well known that the OTP alleges that the Croats in Herceg-Bosnia committed crimes through the vehicle. It's not actually called Crisis Staffs but municipal authorities. But how is that supposed to assist Your Honours in deciding whether the Serbs themselves used set-up and used the Crisis Staff as vehicles for the -- to carry out their joint criminal enterprise? So, Your Honour, we do object to evidence that relates to anything further than what we have already accepted. The Croats did set up Crisis Staffs, and so did the Muslims. Whether we go any further than that, Your Honours, we say is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, does your objection extend beyond -- in terms of the documents, if -- if the documents on which he wishes to put in establish only the fact that you have now conceded, do you still maintain your objection to the route that he proposes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would have thought it was Your Honours who would be objecting. You've spent many, many months telling us not to put in documents that are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This may be true, but the impression I have is that the -- Mr. Zecevic had no reason to believe that the Prosecution would not take issue with the -- his case about the existence, and I keep emphasising like the mere existence of the Crisis Staff, by whatever named called, among these other groupings, leaving it to that and the implications, what I said remain later. But to the extent that Mr. Zecevic is of the view that it is necessary for there to be some documentary foundation to support this fact which the Prosecution does not dispute, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, only in this, Your Honour: If -- if it's for that reason and no other reason apart from the fact that it is not a matter in issue in this case that the other nationalities also set up Crisis Staffs or forms thereof, whatever they call them, because as I understand it in the Croat case, the term "Crisis Staff" does not appear in the indictment against Prlic. No, Your Honours. Although as I say it's a matter for you and the Defence, but it is not a fact in dispute, but anything further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And as to how that's relevant to the issues Your Honours have to decide, I'm not at all clear at the moment, but that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Without in any way giving the impression that the Chamber has formed at this point any view on the importance of these matters, I would, however, be grateful to hear the parties' view on the following possible interpretation of the relevance of the Crisis Staffs formed by the three parties, because if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Zecevic told us yesterday that to the extent in which Crisis Staffs turned out to become tools in the commission of crimes, then the mere establishment of these Crisis Staffs was in itself a factor that would contribute to the commission of crimes. In other words, there need not have been a joint criminal plan from above, because when you give local powers to local authorities under the circumstances which prevailed at the time, it was almost inevitable that crimes would be committed. I may be wrong, but that was what I thought Mr. Zecevic was aiming at yesterday. If I'm wrong, then please enlighten us. But in respect of the fact that Crisis Staffs were established by all three parties, one would then also expect, if I am to pursue the thought that I think Mr. Zecevic was explaining to us yesterday, one would assume that the level of crimes committed by the Crisis Staffs on each side would be approximately the same. At least comparable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if it were to -- if the evidence at the end of the day will show that it was for some reason -- for some reason the level of crimes committed by the Serbian Crisis Staffs was just so much more extended than the crimes committed by the Crisis Staffs of the Croats and the Muslims, then that would be relevant to the assessment of whether or not there was a joint criminal enterprise. I don't know. I may be -- and this is just a question to the parties, because I think it's important that we clarify these matters as the evidence is built up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He will, Your Honour, I think it's Mr. Zecevic to explain what he meant yesterday. I doubt that he could have meant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is partially true, what we've just heard from Judge Harhoff, but only partially, might I say, and here's why: The Defence takes the position that a joint criminal enterprise does not exist in this case. The Defence is also of the view that the establishment of Crisis Staffs, as I've said, is an absolutely legitimate step on the part of all three sides, which stems from the need that arose during that historical period in the former Yugoslavia and especially Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence maintains that that concept which was envisaged by the rules prescribed by the former Yugoslavia was a bad concept. And this is the first time, Your Honours, in 1992, that this concept, which has existed since 1974, in a system of All Peoples Defence and in the legal system of the former Yugoslavia, it's the first time that that concept was ever translated into practice and realised in practice, and once that was done, we arrived at the fact that this concept, in essence, was a self-denying process because it created absolute power in those small segments, in the Crisis Staffs which were set up all over the territory. And then once this power for its own sake was created, power for power's sake without any limit, then of course what happened was the tragedy that we were all witness to. Now, I don't know what more I can say and how I can explain this better, our position better to the Trial Chamber. I don't know if I've been of any assistance. I hope I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the same topic, if you allow me, Your Honours. The position of Zupljanin Defence is the following: First of all, in very brief points, our understanding of the Prosecution case with regard to the issue of Crisis Staff, which they try to support by the testimony of Mrs. Hanson, is the following: Bosnian Serbs at the top level of leadership decided to secretly and contrary to the legislation at that time in Bosnia and Herzegovina create a mechanism to forward the policy of ethnic cleansing and all other crimes which are enlisted in the provisions of the statute of this Tribunal. Point number two of Prosecution theory is that this intention of the top political leadership of Republika Srpska was linked to the local level by way of functioning of Crisis Staffs. At the end of the day, the position of Prosecution is that practically all institutions and all organs of Republika Srpska, including but not limited to like SDS party, army, police, top political leaders and other highly ranking functionaries and also mid-ranking and low-level functionaries, committed on the basis of catch all crime, which is the umbrella crime, which is the concept of JCE. So that is my understanding of this particular part of Prosecution case. Now, the position of the Defence is the following: Point number one: In the general framework of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the nonconstitutional voting against the vital interests of Bosnian Serbs, in accordance with the relevant provisions, Bosnian Serb leadership was actually forced to proceed with the process of disillusion of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at the end, in 1995, under the provisions of the source of the law, which is the Dayton Peace Accord, this right both for Serbian part and for Croatian and Bosnian Muslim part was established. So that was the end of the process of dissolution. In this process and why we are here, in this process individuals committed the crimes, not institutions, not organisations. And furthermore, it is absolutely undisputed fact that -- it is in report of Secretary-General of the UN and president -- many presidents of the Tribunal, and this is practically a logical point of the statute, that only individuals could be held criminally liable. So if Prosecution would like to forward this case under the image of Crisis Staff, this is wrong. This is wrong, Your Honour. Crisis Staff is an institution, is an organisation like SDS, like, I don't know, other governmental institutions. They have to build up their case and to present a case on the basis of the individual criminal responsibility. And that's why, Your Honour, I think that with the testimony of Mrs. Hanson, first of all, and that's why we're doing our job in our cross-examination, we shall show that this OTP approach is not based on the facts, and it's not based on the law. And in my humble opinion, Your Honours, I think wasting the time with political backgrounds, with political interpretation, with -- I don't know, interpretation of certain institutions, bodies and organs, is not the case that should be here. We have two men here allegedly responsible for a very, very serious crimes, and the whole process should be focused on the individual responsibility and elsewhere in all these segments of the case, because we are on the very thin edge to slide into the area of politics, interpretation, et cetera. Thank you very much for your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic, for your useful and interesting commentary. It seems to me that where we are -- that we may have wandered too far afield from what is the issue at hand, namely whether Mr. Zecevic, who happens to have the floor now, can put in as exhibits these documents that deal with the Crisis Staff formed by the Croats and Muslim groups. And having regard to the acceptance of certain facts by the Prosecution, that narrow issue, which is the only thing on which we require to rule, is -- it is probably unnecessary for him to do so, on the other hand, were he to be permitted to do so having regard to what I would have said earlier as to the limited purpose for which it is done, I know no harm is probably done. Mr. Zecevic, how many documents are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe, Your Honours, it's ten documents concerning the Crisis Staffs, the Crisis Staffs of the HDZ, SDA, and others. And I have a number of documents for the Serbian Crisis Staffs, which is a different matter, but if I would be given that opportunity, I wouldn't use the court time for that because I assume that the witness has -- has seen all these documents because those are the documents which we received from the Prosecution, and I will ask her just to comment on maybe one or two and then -- and that is another ten documents at the -- at the maximum. So what we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So a compressed list would suffice for your purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So shall we move on in the interests of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Would the usher escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Hanson. You would not be surprised to learn that your entry into the courtroom was delayed by having to do with some preliminary matters. I remind you you're still on your oath, and I invite Mr. Zecevic to continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off discussing document P438, which was, I'm sure you'll remember, in tab 5 of your binder, and it's the Assembly meeting of Republika Srpska. I read page 285 out to you yesterday of the Serbian text, and in English the page was 315 and 316. Now, Mrs. Hanson, while they're putting up the relevant pages on e-court, I read this document out to you yesterday, or, rather, the excerpt spoken by Mr. Karadzic where he quotes the US news report, and I don't know if you remember -- well, do we need to read it out again today here in the courtroom, or do you remember it? In the Serbian version it was the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I asked you whether you'd read that portion of Mr. Karadzic's presentation, and you said that you couldn't remember having read it but that -- well, then we went on to discuss -- in fact, I claim that in -- that 90 per cent of this meeting of Republika Srpska or the Assembly of Republika Srpska was devoted to a discussion about the conflict between President Karadzic and the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you say you remember that, I'd like to read out another portion. So -- and then I'll ask you a question. On page 314 of the Serbian version, and that is 345 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have that put up on e-court, please. May we have it on the monitor, 314 in Serbian and 345 for the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So before the comment made by Mr. Ninkovic, the last paragraph which begins with "Gentlemen Deputies," and it is General Mladic speaking, and he says: " ... I'm at your disposal, and I propose that you speak your minds as to whether you have confidence in me and in the Main Staff. And please do it by raising your hands. Mr. President, I'm asking for a vote on it," et cetera, et cetera. And then the next sentence reads: "If this Assembly has no confidence in it, please go ahead and say it. You vote on the proposal and I'll support your proposal to ... replace Ratko Mladic. Vote on that too, please. Thank you." Now, Mrs. Hanson, have you read this part of the document before? Do you remember having read it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that here, in actual fact General Mladic is proposing to the Assembly that it should decide whether they're for him or for President Karadzic. That's the bottom line; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the thrust of Mladic's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the next page it's just a brief comment. We don't have to show it, but anyway, Radovan Karadzic says: "People, it's much -- it's serious. It's much more serious than it seems." So I've read this out more for purposes of illustrating my own position and thesis according to which all documents that we are relying on must be interpreted in their historical contents. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll agree with me, too, when I say that it is to be expected that given a situation of this kind, because we're dealing with political survival here, at the very least everybody is trying for its actions and steps to present them in the best light possible, to show that they are important; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be to be expected, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move on to another area, and we're going to discuss part of your report under the heading of "The relationship between police forces." Now, Mrs. Hanson, yesterday, on pages 4455 and 4456 of this transcript you confirmed that for the requirements of this case and these proceedings and at the request of your employer, the OTP, you added to your report a part under the title of the relationship between the Crisis Staffs and the police forces, and that's this particular section. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very brief section or part of the previous report dealt with the police, but I expanded that into an entire section. I think I just had two paragraphs or so in the previous version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that you expanded this. It relates to this portion of your report; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now you will remember that yesterday when we discussed the matter I suggested -- I put it to you that in my opinion that part that was supplemented in an unobjective way or rather in such a way as to incorporate it into your already existing conclusions, but you didn't agree with me on that point and you responded, and if I'm paraphrasing you properly, I think you said that you studied the documents and that you found nothing in those documents which would be contrary to the conclusions you had made already and that that is why you stayed with the same conclusions. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's analyse this and I'll show you how your positions and your conclusions are completely wrong. I'm sure you know that the police is part of the state administration; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever read the law governing state administration of Republika Srpska that is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the law on general administrative procedure is about?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Well, I can tell from the title, but I'm not familiar with the law if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the law on general administrative proceedings regulates the principles of work of the Ministry of the Interior as a basic law?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not surprised to learn it, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, that is to say two days ago, on page 4386 of the transcript, you were shown Exhibit P439, and I'm just telling you that for purposes of reference. I'm not going to display it, not to lose time. Anyway, you commented on this with my colleague, and you told us about what Karadzic said in a text when you said that the police has to be responsible to the civilian authorities. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From the context of your report, I gain the impression that you see something bad in what he said when he said that the police has to be responsible to the civilian authorities. Am I wrong or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not bad. That's a value judgement. I don't -- judgements about what's good or bad, I just see what -- trying to interpret the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mrs. Hanson, now, this sentence saying that the police must be responsible to the civilian authorities, you interpreted that within the context of responsibility on the part of the police to the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the new structures the Serbian state, which include the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, Mrs. Hanson, to the best of your knowledge and in your opinion, to whom in principle is the police responsible in other states, for example, here in the Netherlands or in England? Isn't it true that the police is also responsible to the civil authorities because the police is in fact in all civilised countries part of the state administration? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's certainly my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you know that this fact was additionally pointed out and was particularly pertinent in Yugoslavia at that time because in the Communist days the police was abused to settle accounts with dissidents, people who didn't -- were not of the same view as the powers that be were. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know about the security forces, yes. I don't want -- I can't make the connection here to -- that this is a pertinent issue right here, but I will agree that the police were, yes, they are involved in the repression of dissidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you know that in the former Yugoslavia the police existed, that it dealt with people who had different thoughts. There was the Stazi in Germany, for example, and in Romania the Securitatea service, let alone the KGB in the Soviet Union and so on and so forth. So I'm sure you're aware of all this; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, madam, then I'm sure you know that the democratic parties such as the parties that we're discussing here, the Serbian Democratic Party, the Croatian Democratic Party, and the Party of Democratic Action, by definition were adversaries to a one-party Communist system, and by the same token all their members were arrested, persecuted, and so on and so forth. I'm sure you know that; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware that the leaders of the Serbian -- Serbian Democratic Party, for example, were arrested and persecuted as leaders of national parties, because by the time they were founded, they were founded at the time of multi-party elections, so I don't see them as persecuted in the former system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that relevant, but certainly they were persecuted before there were substantive changes made and the opening up of Yugoslavia and its democratization and so on and so forth. And when in the 1990's the multi-party system was introduced, they were persecuted before that and I wasn't referring to the leaders, I was referring to the members of these parties but it's not that important, let's move on. Let's move on to something you discussed here in your report. In paragraph 83 of your report - I've already asked you this, I believe - you looked at the law governing interm affairs of Republika Srpska, and you analysed certain articles or, rather, three articles of that particular law; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mrs. Hanson, do you know that the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska was established in the following way: A division was made of the previous MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all this in keeping with the principles established in the plan by -- of the European Union, better known in public as the Cutileiro Plan. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my understanding how it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will certainly agree with me that the MUP of Republika Srpska was established on the basis of the existing public security stations and some of the existing security services centre -- I see that my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Sorry to interrupt, but at the start of Ms. Hanson's testimony, she was asked whether she was an expert on the structure and functioning of the RS MUP, and she said that was outside of her area of expertise. So I don't see how these questions are relevant to her, how she's able to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked Mrs. Hanson at the very beginning about her area of expertise, and we established that she was not an expert for this. That's not what I'm asking her. I'm asking her about paragraph 83 of her report as well as paragraphs 80 through 89 of her report. They are under the heading relations with police stations. That's the only section of the report I'm focusing on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, inasmuch as you're asking her questions about her report, you may proceed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So I asked you, madam, do you know that the MUP of Republika Srpska was formed from already existing police stations and some security services centres with the proviso that the regional organisation was arranged in keeping with the law on the interior, the Law on Internal Affairs? You've read that law. I suppose you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I read those parts of the law which pertain to relations with municipal authorities. On the formation of the MUP, I haven't read extensively on that. I noticed that both in Variant A and B and in later documents they did not always take over existing police stations, because in some municipalities those were not in the Serb-populated areas, so they made their own new police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It seems I did not understand you correctly then. You mean to say that Variants A and B, you mean to say that the MUP of Republika Srpska was created through Crisis Staffs in Variants A and B, and that the police stations of the Serbian MUP were established in some municipalities where Serbs did not live? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You said that did I know that the MUP of Republika Srpska was formed from already existing police stations, and my understanding both from the documents from March, April 1992 and from the Variant A-B instructions is that in some places it was formed from already existing police stations. In other places they made new police stations. They didn't take over the already existing ones. And that would be in places where the existing police stations which they did not take over were not in Serb-dominant areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now I understand. I'm sorry. However, these police stations that were established were established pursuant to the law, not pursuant to any instructions or Variants A and B. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see Crisis Staffs in some places helping set up new police stations. I do not see them citing the laws under which they were formed. I was looking at Crisis Staff documents, not at the documents of each individual police station. So I don't know their own internal procedures and on what basis they were -- on what laws they were citing or what -- what procedures they were following. I have seen, as I showed in the speech by Karadzic in March, at the March Assembly session, it was seen as one of the steps in the takeovers, and the Crisis Staffs were leading those steps, were taking those steps on the ground. So although once the -- perhaps the territorial division was set out by the law, I see the Crisis Staffs helping the creation of these forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, let us make this simpler. Would you agree with me that the Law on Internal Affairs, which also stipulated the territorial organisations of various organs of the interior, was adopted in March 1993 by the Assembly of the Serbian People? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We agreed yesterday that at that time, starting with January 1992, the Republika Srpska was in existence, and since February the same year it had its own constitution; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now when you are quoting Mr. Karadzic, when he says in March -- when he speaks about the establishment of these police bodies, aren't these steps in the establishment of state organs? How did you imagine an established state that does not proceed to form its state agencies, including police stations and security centres? Would that be imaginable for a state to fail to do that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's completely logical that a state would form its agencies, including police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's precisely what I'm trying to say. Madam, let us now analyse your principal conclusion here in section 83 where you say that the municipal police station received in parallel tasks from the Ministry of the Interior and from Municipal Assemblies, and it was answerable to them. Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, "report to," is how I put it, but, yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then in support of that you quoted these three articles, 27, 31, and 32. That document was shown to you. It's tab 32, I believe, the Law on Internal Affairs. In e-court it's 65 ter 53, but since we have an understanding that these documents should be introduced as stipulated by the parties, it has no P or D designation. Articles 27, 31 and 32 are all on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 4 in e-court, in Serbian. I suppose it's page 4 or 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Hanson, it is your position that the municipal police station, under the law received assignments both from the Ministry of the Interior and the Municipal Assembly and that it reported to the Municipal Assembly and was answerable to the Municipal Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was answerable to the Municipal Assembly and to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And to support that you quote Article 27. Let us analyse it. Article 27 relates municipal regulations, it says, In addition to the activities and tasks set out in the rules on the internal organisation of the ministry a public security station shall implement also regulations passed by the Municipal Assembly and relating to law and order and road safety, as well as other regulations in the domain of internal affairs that have been passed by the Municipal Assembly. First, the regulations passed by Municipal Assemblies, as you can see in the last sentence, are enacted under the authority envisaged in the Law on Internal Affairs. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So when it says, Regulations relating to law and order, do you know what is meant? Can you give us an example or shall I give an example and then you can confirm or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll do that. These municipal regulations are, for instance, this: Whether catering establishments and shops may be open until 10.30 p.m. or until midnight. That's one. Two, whether outdoor cafes where live bands play can have these bands playing until 11.00 p.m., until midnight, or 3.00 in the morning. Whether alcohol is served in cafes before 10.00 a.m. or not. That's the kind of regulation a Municipal Assembly can adopt. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the kind of regulations, but I see Crisis Staffs acting in the name of Municipal Assemblies taking much more sweeping actions or -- more significant decisions than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, please. We're now talking about your position, your conclusion where you say that the police station received assignments and tasks both from the Assembly and the MUP and that it was written in the law. Now I want, together with you, to analyse these articles of the law which you invoke to show you that you are absolutely mistaken. I'm not talking about the de facto situation. I'm talking about the legal situation, because you found in your report that there is a legal ground for your claim that police stations are answerable to Municipal Assemblies and implement the Assemblies' decisions. Furthermore, this article says, Another kind of regulation passed by the Municipal Assembly relates to road safety. I'll give you another example. That is a situation, for instance, when although it was prescribed at the state level that the minimum speed is 50 kilometres, in a certain town where you have a spa or a school or a kindergarten, something, another speed, 30 kilometres, is stipulated, or perhaps speed bumps are installed. That is the kind of regulation a Municipal Assembly can pass, and then the public security station, exercising its authority in that area is duty-bound to enforce them. Those are the only regulations that public security stations had to enforce that had been passed about by a Municipal Assembly. Everything else enforced by public security stations was written in the law. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note that the law says "along with other regulations." So I can't agree that those are the only kind which the Municipal Assembly could pass. The law stipulates that other regulations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, aren't we going down a -- a troublesome part inasmuch as the witness was proffered as an expert on Crisis Staffs. She has stated the obvious on several occasions that she is not a lawyer, and these detailed questions which, as I understand it, involve the interpretation and application of laws, and they -- aren't they off the track, so to speak, in terms of the competence of this witness and the purpose for which she was proffered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, the conclusion of this witness as written in her report is that the police, that is the police station, is answerable to and enforces the tasks given them by the Assembly, and in support of that claim she quotes these three articles. It is quite obvious that she does not understand to what these three articles apply. That's her claim. If Mrs. Hanson withdraws that conclusion here now I will desist, but I have to question Mrs. Hanson and educate her to show her that the basis she -- she used and the conclusion she made, all that is based on a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters for overlapping with Mr. Zecevic. I would have thought, though, with respect, Mr. Zecevic, that as with any other witness, as with any other bit of evidence, the -- not everything that is contained in the report, which is what the Prosecution's relying on here, is accepted, every letter, and that the -- a person reading the report, to be specific here, the Chamber, would, as they go through it, mentally discard or disregard things which are clearly outside the competence of the -- in this case the person writing the report. She isn't a lawyer, so as a lawyer she would get certain things wrong. She -- there's the context in which she said certain things, but not being a lawyer, it's obviously wrong. That may be a -- the logical and fair conclusion which the Chamber may reach. So I come back to asking why -- whether it is necessary to go down the road of challenging her on all of these details which, as I said, at the end of the day probably wouldn't make a deference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I see that perhaps it's time for the break now. Maybe it's a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have three minutes. Can you make use of those three minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I wonder if I could just add a comment to what's been said perhaps to help matters. That is, I think that what is contained in the report on this point is pretty clear, and what Mr. Zecevic is saying has been said in this report goes well beyond what she does actually say in her report. If you look at paragraph 83, she says: "The RS Law on Internal Affairs stipulated the police's obligations to the municipal civilian authority," and she cites three articles. That's it. She doesn't go into -- the report doesn't go into the sort of detail which Mr. Zecevic seems to be saying that it does go into, the sort of minute detail which he's been putting to her. That is clearly is beyond what she has said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But with all due respect, Your Honours, the last -- I was referring to the last comment of Ms. Hanson's report where she confirmed right now that she stated that in the report, which says -- I don't have the English copy with me here. I have the Serbian, so I will read in Serbian. [Interpretation] "Thus the police station received tasks both from the Ministry of the Interior and the Municipal Assembly and reported to them or was answerable to them." Mrs. Hanson confirmed this, and I am just trying to ask Mrs. Hanson on what basis she concluded that. She said on the basis of Articles 27, 31, and 32.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's bad translation, then. It's not what the English says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it's better that we take the break now so we can clarify tis matter in order not to lose time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, I put it to you and claim that Article 31, which you are interpreting here, are interpreting erroneously, because the article prescribes that it is the duty of the public security station to provide information to the local organs about the security situation and that that is a rational and normal situation, because the local organs have an interest, of course, in seeing the state of crime on the territory, and juvenile delinquency, and so on and so forth, or drug-related problems. I also claim that Article 32, which once again you are interpreting wrongly, is -- provides the possibility of local organs going to the MUP seat, MUP headquarters, with their own proposals and suggestions, but that ultimately comes under the auspices of the MUP. That is to say, it is up to the MUP at its headquarters whether it's going to adopt those proposals or not and this relates to the suggestions of the type by which they say that this is because of juvenile delinquency that they're having the problems of that, or drugs. They need more inspectors dealing in that kind of thing at the public security station or police station. And that is why I am saying, Mrs. Hanson, that your conclusions in paragraph 83 are absolutely unfounded. Do you have any comments to make to that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 32, I agree, does not have -- I would say, rather -- not that I have misinterpreted, but it really doesn't have bearing on the issue. In fact, it is -- I would say that Article 32 shows indeed that the ministry has the ultimate say on those matters, that it's merely a consultative relationship between the Municipal Assembly and the ministry headquarters on those matters. So I think we can put Article 32 to the side. As far as the Article 31, I make no judgement about whether it's rational and normal or not, but I simply state that if the security stations submit reports and information, that to me is not -- it is not wrong then to say that the station shall report to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, I think that at the very beginning, and I think my colleague objected rightly so, and so did the Presiding Judge, Judge Hall, but anyway, I think at the beginning that we clarified the matter and established that you do not have the necessary qualifications for interpreting legal provisions in the laws. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed that I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you have the necessary expertise for interpreting legal provisions. Yes or no? In your opinion, in your own opinion.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that all the conclusions that you make and present here in paragraphs 80, 81, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 89, which do not relate to the factual situation but to legal provisions we can leave aside and forget because you don't have the necessary qualifications for making those assessments. You don't have the expertise to make those evaluations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that only paragraph 83 relates to legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. Mrs. Hanson, I'm trying to make a distinction here. Let's start this way: I agree with you that in practice the Crisis Staffs took, over to a significant extent, powers and authority that did not belong to them, that they commanded the police, that they issued orders to the police, that they appointed chiefs of police and other police employees, but this was only the de facto situation. I'm not questioning the de facto situation here. What I am questioning and challenging is your assertion that that situation was the result of legal provisions or laws or any other provisions which have anything to do with the Ministry of the Interior. That is what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree with you that the Crisis Staffs commanded police, issued orders to the police, appointed chiefs of police and other police employees. You say that this is powers and authority that did not belong to them. I -- as I've indicated from the start, I find no laws specifying the powers and authority of the Crisis Staffs. I have the instructions for 26 April, for example, which would not appear to limit the power of the Crisis Staffs in those areas, as you say. So I can't agree that -- I have no basis for saying that the powers and authorities did or did not belong to them, but de facto they did that. I do not say that all of what they did was based on that one article, but I think that article gives a starting point, a way -- an indication of the relationship between the municipal authorities and the police, that -- that the police were not completely separate from the Municipal Assembly, that they only had the chain of command through the ministry. I want to show that there are points at the municipal level where the police received taskings from and reported to the Assembly. Then the Assembly is represented by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, there are a number of elements and points here. First of all, your assertions which you want to seriously state here, that is -- that they are instructions Variants A and B above the law governing the Ministry of Internal Affairs as a legal act. Yes or no? Are they over and above the law?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're outside it. They were issued as party instructions long before the Bosnian Serbs wrote their Law on Internal Affairs. So by the time the law was written, I would say A and B was superseded by events. So I don't see that they're in relationship. I think that as far as the law of the land of Bosnia at the time, I would say they were -- again I'm not a lawyer, but I would say that forming parallel municipal organs and secretly arming and secretly removing things from commodity reserves was outside the law of the land and the Law on Internal Affairs at the time they were written.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, all these facts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to wait for the interpretation to finish before he begins putting his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- I accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, did you hear the reminder from the interpreters to avoid overlapping?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. I forgot to put my headset on, and I'm listening to the English, but, yes, I do apologise. And I also apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, all these facts which I have confirmed, among other things, that is to say that the Crisis Staffs were outside their powers of authority. They superseded and went beyond their powers and authorisations and so on. They did issue orders to the police. They did appoint chiefs. They appointed chiefs who had never set foot in the police force ever. They were appointed chiefs of security stations. They issued orders to them. They issued provisions and regulations. I don't question any of that. So those facts, the facts you're talking about, all that is going on after the law was passed on internal affairs and after it came into force. So look at your report, madam. In your report, you quote examples from April, May, June, possibly July. That means that at that time, the law was in existence. It was in force. How then are you able to say that the instructions and Variant A and B was applicable despite the fact that the Law on Internal Affairs existed, was in force? And if I've understood your assertions correctly, it was even stronger as a legal act, a legal document, than the Law on Internal Affairs according to you. So how can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, when I said "instructions," I think I was referring -- I can't see the text now, but I think I was referring to Djeric's instructions of 26 April, 1992 which would be after that law, but I'm not a lawyer and I am not here to judge the legality of the facts on the ground and to say which law was applicable. I cannot find, as I said, anything that sets out in legal terms the limits of the authority of the Crisis Staffs. I only can -- am describing what I have seen in the evidence, and I'm not trying to judge whether -- how closely they followed the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, I claim that you didn't have in mind the instructions of the 26th of April, although we'll come to those instructions in due course, very shortly, in fact. I claim that you were referring to Variant A and B because you said that those instructions or that instruction existed before the law was enforced. You did say that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you were asking about its relationship, was it outside the law or something. Yes, that's what I was talking about then, but I thought you were referring to an earlier reference. But yes, when you asked me about Variant A being outside the law, I said it was apples and oranges, irrelevant to the Law on Internal Affairs because it's from a different period. It's from December and -- December 1991, and obviously the law wasn't passed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you remember us commenting on that yesterday? We commented on the instructions and Variant A and B, and on the very last page in point 2 we read out together the responsibility provided for for all the organs, that in their work and activities they should respect in -- absolutely all the federal and republican laws that are not in contravention with the federal law. Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when I asked you whether you thought that this was a dead letter on paper, you said no, it was expected of those organs, to respect the law in other words; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that question. I didn't understand it in those terms. Which organs are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the organs to whom the instructions were sent through Variant A and B, that is to say the Crisis Staffs and other organs which were set up subsequently, the various assemblies, Municipal Assemblies, executive boards or whatever. That was what we were discussing yesterday, remember?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, as I say, I simply do not recall that particular question, but would I say, as I said before, although there is that stipulation that they should observe all federal laws, I would say that some of the tasks in the 19 December instructions are in fact in contradiction to the federal or republican laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right then. Then tell me on the basis of which expertise of yours and knowledge of yours can you tell me that some of the tasks which were given in the instructions of the 19th of December are in contravention of federal or republican laws? What -- on what grounds do you say that? Your knowledge of those laws, your expertise to provide opinions about whether or not certain organs acted in conformity with the law or not, or some third reason, some third grounds?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would base my answer on my -- that of the general knowledge of an informed person that to form -- to secretly remove items from commodity reserves sounds to a layperson, a non-lawyer, like it's against the law. Perhaps it is not, but it's just simply on the common sense of an educated person, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't agree with you there. It's only if you have a stand taken before, if you've already made your decision. You're putting me in an impossible situation here, madam. On the one hand you're saying that you don't have enough knowledge and expertise to comment on that, and whereas on the other hand you make certain claims and assertions and state that something was not in conformity with the law, and now I can't even show you some of the legal provisions by which I would confirm that you are not right, that you're wrong. That's the predicament I'm in. And I claim that -- well, when you claim that you can understand on the basis of intelligence and reasoning is not sufficient to interpret certain legal provisions and questions as to whether certain organs are working in keeping with the law and provisions or not. Madam, let's focus on something else that you said, and I'd like to hear your explanations. In paragraph 89, you actually say -- the substance of that paragraph is that you say that all the organs associated themselves on a state level. I think you said that somewhere, paraphrasing paragraph 89. Anyway, you say that they all joined together at a state level because the Ministry of the Interior was a member of the government. Do you remember having said that at some point?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if I understand you correctly, it is then your assertion that -- I assume also on the basis of something you keep mentioning, the 26th of April instructions signed by Prime Minister Djeric, your assertions that the government did have control over the Crisis Staffs; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that I assert they had control. They issued instructions to, they gave some orders to, they assisted, they received reports from. On control, I think you'd have to define a little more carefully in terms of what you mean. They issued orders to, yes, and received reports from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would call that control. If you give somebody orders and receive reports from that person and perhaps can take steps against someone if they do not act in accordance to your orders, I would term that control. Wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- abstractly, yes, I would term that control. On the question of taking steps against those, I haven't seen evidence of the government taking those steps at the time, so if that's -- but I -- I think we're pretty much agreed on what constitutes control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mrs. Hanson, that apart from a single -- one single report which is mentioned at one of the government meetings and that the first neighbouring municipality from the place where the government was situated at that point, and I'm referring to Novo Sarajevo, not a single other report ever of the Crisis Staff was presented -- of any of the Crisis Staffs was presented at a government meeting, nor did you ever see some sort of report of that kind in written form.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the report to the National Security Council which I believe was a joint meeting with the government at which they received a report on the work of Crisis Staffs. We have no more specific information on that. We have requested from the RS authorities if it's possible to identify that report. We've never received anything. And, yes, there's a report of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo, that of the Crisis Staff in Foca, said he made a report to the council of ministers which since there was no Council of Ministers at the time, I take to be the ministers' National Security Council sitting together with the government, but that is not specified by him. So the only report I have seen is Novo Sarajevo, but I have evidence of other kinds of reporting. Also, we see the government in their minutes have received requests for funds from Crisis Staffs. I have not seen those written requests, but I would believe the government would expect something in writing. Also, Rajlovac. I've seen them writing to the Rajlovac War Commission writing to the government. So that's another written item. Unfortunately, it was before -- that came to my attention after this report was written, so I don't know if I can include it or not, refer you to it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, I'll go back to a comment I made yesterday. I put a very specific question to you. Now, from your answer that has taken up half a page we come back to the same thing. Your answer to my question is in fact yes. Have you ever seen any single written report to a government meeting in Novo Sarajevo? Your answer was no. So the only report, written report, you've ever seen is that one. Now, the one that went to the National Security Council and some other organs you expect to be able to understand that, but the only report you saw was the Novo Sarajevo report. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Let's place things back in context. Is it true, and please give me a brief answer, preferably yes or no, is it true that the National Security Council issued recommendations to the government to adopt some sort of instructions on the work of War Presidency and War Executive Councils on 22 April 1992? That's paragraph 31 of your report. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the government really issued such instructions on the 26th of April? It's P70, and the title is "Instructions for the Work of Crisis Staffs." Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that tomorrow, on the 27th -- sorry, the next day, 27 April, at the joint session of the National Security Council and the government, it was noted that the 26 April instructions were not detailed enough for local authorities? And you talk about that in paragraph 35 of your report. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption is it's the 26 April instructions. They say that more detailed instructions need to be issued. I can't say for sure that they're referring to Djeric's. That's the logical inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And isn't it true that three days from the instructions, 26 April, which is Exhibit P70, as I said, titled "Instructions for the Work of Crisis Staffs," the government, the same organ that issued the instructions, withdraws the instructions and says "Consider it null and void," in capital letters. It's P86. If we can call it up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it. It should be 65 ter 105. That is the document I asked for. Maybe my reference is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It's P186.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter may have misheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were doing your research for the report, did you find this document in your set of documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I discuss it in footnote 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You're talking about the document rescinding the instructions of the 26th of April, three days after they were adopted. You mention it in a footnote but nowhere in the text; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because I had reason to believe that the document as issued on the 26th of April was in fact received and implemented. I'd be happy to explain it in greater detail if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No need, madam. Just tell me, are you seriously trying to tell us and the Trial Chamber that the Crisis Staffs, as you say in your report, received the instructions of the 26th April but did not receive this letter withdrawing the instructions? Are you seriously trying to say that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no basis on which to say whether they did or did not receive the instructions withdrawing it. I can, as I said, explain further my --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No need, madam. Documents speak for themselves. If there is no basis for you to confirm that they received this document rescinding the instructions, then there's no need to discuss it anymore. Other witnesses will come who will confirm the facts. Among other things, we heard another witness here who was chairman of one of the Crisis Staffs and who explicitly said --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Objecting here, having my colleague putting transcripts of what other witnesses have said to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I remember your guidelines correctly, it is allowed to put to a witness what another witness has said without naming the other witness or giving any of his identifying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but you can't just simply put the previous testimonies of a witness to a witness on the stand and invite him or her to contradict it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to elicit a comment from this witness on the claim of a prior witness that he had never received the instructions or acted upon them. I wanted to hear this witness's comment, but if you think I should not be allowed to do that, of course I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps it's possible -- Mr. Dobbyn, you had an intervention, a further intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. That's what the witness has said, and what is this witness supposed to say about that? It's just the words of two different witnesses. Where can that take us really?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may have your indulgence. The guidelines for leading and introducing evidence, September 2009, para 22: "The party conducting cross-examination may put evidence given by a prior witness on the condition that the witness's identity is not revealed. Parties are reminded not to comment on the credibility of other witnesses." My understanding is that I may put to this witness some prior evidence or testimony and elicit a comment without identifying the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So long as the question is phrased to elicit a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I said I wanted to do, but the objection came before I even stated my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, one of the presidents of one of the Crisis Staffs from a territory you mentioned many times in your report testified here before, and he said explicitly he had never seen any instructions, received any instructions, or needed any, in fact, in order to establish the Crisis Staff because the law was abundantly clear, and that he never reported to anyone in any way. Do you have a comment?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere in my report do I say that every Crisis Staff received these instructions, nor that every Crisis Staff reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is an issue which I believe has been raised in the past, and that is that if a transcript -- testimony is going to be put to the witness then we need to have the reference for that. Otherwise, we can't follow. We don't know exactly what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had not anticipated that this would become reason for an objection so I don't have a reference ready. Of course I can find it. As far as I'm concerned, I can even withdraw the question. Perhaps that is the simplest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, in paragraph 38, you not only claim that the government allegedly exerted control or some sort of control over the Crisis Staff, you claim that the leadership took steps to make Crisis Staffs legal and official and to reinforce their links with the centre. Is that correct? That's your paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 39, you state that the government, already on 23rd May 1992, proposed to abolish Crisis Staffs. That's P217. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And establish War Presidencies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that's written in document P217? That's the government's meeting of 23rd May 1992. It only says, I believe, to abolish Crisis Staffs. Shall we call it up in e-court?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asserting that that's what I write there. If we call it up, if you -- I haven't read that reference in many years. If you say it says only -- abolish Crisis Staffs, yes. I was not -- I was asserting -- just trying to correct the sentence as written as -- as you read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was the situation with the Crisis Staffs, roughly: On 26 April, the government issues instructions, on the 30th, it withdraws the instructions, and just three weeks later the government advocates that Crisis Staffs be abolished; correct? That's the chronology?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I would have a lot more to say on the subject of the withdrawal of the instructions, but I agree with the first and last items of your chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To continue the chronology: The Presidency of Republika Srpska, on 24 May 1992, issues instructions on the work of presidencies in municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then seven days later, on 31 May 1992, that instruction was replaced by the presidential decision of Radovan Karadzic, and the reference I have for that is 65 ter 145. Correct? That's the decision by President Radovan Karadzic of 31st May 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us come back to your paragraph 38 again. If the government asks for the Crisis Staffs to be abolished and the Presidency right the next day issues instructions on the work of presidencies and seven days later the president confirms that instruction by his own decision, isn't it then true that the central authorities wanted to abolish Crisis Staffs and establish other organs in their place rather than to reinforce them or, as you put it, make them official or legal?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps some of the confusion arises in my first -- the first sentence of paragraph 38 where Crisis Staffs there I'm using more, as I indicate I do, as a general umbrella term for these extraordinary collective municipal bodies, because I see a continuity among all these organs. I see Crisis Staffs becoming War Presidencies simply by changing their name. I don't see a significant difference between Crisis Staffs and War Presidency in operation. Therefore, I see these all as moves to get a formal status for these already existing collective municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, the authorities such as the Assembly or the Executive Board envisaged by the constitution are unable to operate because of the war. That's why Crisis Staffs are established. We see then that Crisis Staffs were abolished and the organs of Presidency take their place. Again, we're not talking about continuity. We're only talking about different bodies. You seem to agree with me that the intention was to abolish Crisis Staffs. I mean, the intention of central authorities was to abolish Crisis Staffs and to form Presidency. Again, I'm not talking about continuity or discontinuity.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that they are changing -- abolishing Crisis Staffs and forming Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that happened in end May. Less than ten days later, on 10th of June, the same president, Karadzic, changes that decision to form Presidencies and issues the decision to form War Commissions that are completely different bodies in terms of composition and membership. That's 65 ter 151. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He issues another decision. To the best of my recollection, although I would have to see the decision itself, he makes no reference to the 31 May decision. So I couldn't exactly say that he changes that decision. He issues another that appears to be contradictory or to be a change of the first one. And, yes, I agree that the composition as laid out in the decision is quite different from a war Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, you claim in paragraph 44, I believe, of your report that the reason for that was to ensure better central control over the work of bodies on the ground. Isn't it in fact the only logical and the only accurate explanation that all these changes occurred because neither Mr. Karadzic nor anyone else was able to establish any control over Crisis Staffs or any other bodies at the local level?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's analyse that a little. In April and May, in that territory there are Serbian municipalities. Authorities slowly take shape, and in the meantime the conflicts begin. In some of the municipalities where conflict has already broken out, the Crisis Staffs already exist. In others, they will be formed later in May and June when the armed insurgency of Muslim and Croat forces begin. Is this indeed the context where all this is happening?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have trouble with the last two -- two items in the last part of your statement. I don't -- I'm not aware of Crisis Staffs being formed in May and June. By then I would usually see a war Presidency formed. And I would also not describe the events as the armed insurgency of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, madam, of paragraph 30, namely the footnote where you state: "The establishment of Crisis Staff of Bihac, 22nd May 1992; the establishment of Bosanska Dubica Crisis Staff, 17 June 1992; Bosanska Gradiska, 30th September --"

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the footnote linked to your paragraph 36, footnote 50.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, you're right. So those are Crisis Staffs formed in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mrs. Hanson, I put it to you that the government gave instructions to the Crisis Staffs and then withdrew them because these instructions had absolutely no effect because the government did not have the authority. That's why all this is raised to a higher level, the level of the Presidency. And then Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, as member of the Presidency, issues instructions on the 24th of May, and then Karadzic confirms that in the form of a presidential decision on the 31st of May. And since not even this presidential decision yields any significant effect, on the 10th of June he issues the decision on the establishment of War Commissions. That's the third instruction. The whole concept is then changed. The name is changed. Not in order to strengthen these bodies but to achieve some degree of control over these bodies at local level. That is the real intent.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't think that's the intent for the letter withdrawing the instructions, because it names that it's an incomplete text. And judging on where and how we see War Commissions formed, I don't see that this is his intent to supersede the 31st May decision simply because we see the two bodies co-existing in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't think, do you, that the central authorities form one body and then another body with the intention of having them co-exist.
