Isn't this in fact proof of the impotence of the central authorities? Isn't it proof that those who assumed power within one body don't want to let go of that power? You have Crisis Staffs in places where Municipal Assemblies had already been formed in autumn 1992, and the Assembly of Republika Srpska had to pass a decree in December 1992 to abolish Crisis Staffs. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see anything from the Assembly in December 1992 abolishing Crisis Staffs. There is a decision of abolishing War Commissions, but I see nothing on the abolishing of Crisis Staffs then. And I think that had Karadzic intended to have War Commissions replaced, Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies everywhere, we could see more decisions on forming War Commissions. We have decisions signed by Karadzic on forming War Commissions in a few municipalities. So I think if there were an intent to form them everywhere, we would see those documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you seriously think that it's the job of the President of Republika Srpska, the president of the Presidency, to determine who will be at the head of the Crisis Staff of Sekovic municipality? It's 1D01-0688.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose, madam, when you said what you just said a moment ago in your previous answer that you meant documents like this where President Karadzic confirms the appointments of members of the War Commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you again. Don't you think it is a bit absurd that the president of the Presidency would have to confirm the appointments of the War Commission in Sekovici municipality? Doesn't this show, in fact, that he has no control and he's trying to assert his authority in this way by signing, himself, a completely insignificant paper? Perhaps not insignificant but certainly a document that does not really deserve the signature of a president.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the numerous, numerous appointments of War Presidency in 1995, late 1994 and 1995, are also signed by Karadzic. So I take it more to be an artefact of the way the state administration operated that this kind of a document from the Presidency requires his signature. I don't believe from this document that he himself chose those members. Quite the contrary. That's what his commissioner was for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with the assertions that the reason for which -- well, things that have been said in court here, that the reason for which the decision on the founding of War Commissions is the fact that Mr. Karadzic was complaining that he didn't have control over the territorial organs, or, rather, that nobody has any control over the territorial organs? Would you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam -- Mrs. Hanson, let's summarise this situation concerning the Crisis Staffs and the other organs which are the subject of your report. I put it to you that the Crisis Staffs came into being on the basis of a concept, the committee of a total national defence and social self-protection, and that because of that, on all sides at the same time, in 1991 and 1992, they were set up. In 1991, that is to say before variant -- Variants A and B, and according to certain information on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are over 950 Crisis Staffs on all sides and throughout the republic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs which are the subject of my report are not the same as those 900 and however many Crisis Staffs. We're talking about two -- they're simply not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's interesting that the Prosecution accepted a moment ago, at the beginning of our -- these proceedings today, that that was one and the same thing, but never mind. I'm not going to belabour the point and comment. Tell us, please, I put it to you that those Crisis Staffs, those organs, were no specific feature invented by the Serb side. They weren't any secret organs of a shadow government or any such mystifications which you claim in your report, but that they were the result of needs in view of the fact that in the former Yugoslavia central power and authority had toppled at all levels, the federal level, the republican level, and that it no longer functioned. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you further, madam, that as the situation was what it was, that the power and authority at federal republican level was not functioning properly and that all sides turned to a concept that existed in legislation and practice, that is to say the concept of total national defence and social self-protection, and that is where their uniformity comes from on all sides, the Muslim, the Croat, and the Serb side, that is, holding certain territory at a given period in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that all sides turned to the concept of these committees. I agree with that part of your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree that in substance there was nothing criminal in the setting up of the Crisis Staffs, because the concept itself and the remit, authorisation, composition and role was stipulated by law? It was only that all their or organs, beginning with the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the different parties, the different organs gave different names to them. Instead of calling them committees, they called them Crisis Staffs. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I'd like to interject. I believe what's been put to the witness now is a matter for Your Honours and not for her to comment on. In addition, I haven't wanted to interrupt until this point but beyond this particular question as well I believe quite properly my colleague is putting his case or the differences to the witness. However, these have been wrapped up in several questions in one, and if he is putting his case to her, I would ask also that it be single questions rather than combinations of questions and statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You do of course appreciate that in inviting the witness on the stand to comment on the relevant aspects of your case it isn't helpful if you, as Mr. Dobbyn says, ask multiple -- compound questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- [Interpretation] In keeping with Rule 90(H), I believe it is, I am putting to the witness what I am duty-bound to do following the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There's no question about that. It's just that if the perception is from somebody else, in this case Mr. Dobbyn, that the way it is put is in a way that it is unhelpful to the witness to understand it because the witness is not going to be -- if she's asked several questions and when any answer is meaningless because you don't know what part she's accepting and what part she's not. And that's why I prefaced my comment to you by saying you agree. So it's something that you -- a rule that you well know. It's simply a matter of your applying it and phrasing your question appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I understand, Your Honour, and I will follow on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, my last question a moment ago was the following: Do you agree with me that there is nothing criminal in the creation of the Crisis Staffs in view of the concept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I renew my objection. The first point I made during my objection that this is a matter for Your Honours to decide. This is not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would -- I would appreciate if at least my learned colleague will wait until I pose the question. Then probably the reason why he's objecting might not be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, may I intervene, because I dealt with this matter. I said, in the absence of the witness, but I have made the Prosecution's positions clear about whether or not the establishment of the Crisis Staffs was criminal is a matter of evidence for Your Honours. It's not appropriate for the witness to give her view on whether the establishment was criminal. She's interpreting the evidence as an expert and saying, these are the conclusions I come to as to what happened. The criminality or otherwise of that is not a matter for her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, I would have thought that the 40 minutes that we spent at the beginning of today's sitting would have made -- would have taken this off the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to -- well, it is my duty to question the Prosecution's case and assertion that he is developing through his witnesses, because I have to have the basis for my closing arguments. If I have not challenged and questioned the positions and conclusions of a Prosecution witness, then tomorrow when the time comes at the end of the day when I come to make my closing arguments I won't have sufficient arguments to present before the Trial Chamber for you to be able to deliberate. So that is why I'm forced to question this witness just as I would any other, in keeping with the rules of this Tribunal and at all times and in each case to challenge the correctness of those positions. So I can't give up on that role, nor does my conscious allow me to or my professional integrity allow me to give up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Dobbyn is expecting you to do that. It just occurs to me, and unless I misunderstand Mr. Dobbyn's objection, this is the basis of his objection, that the conclusions which you -- well, the comments that you're seeking to elicit from the witness in the way you phrase your questions are bound up with the -- what, as I said at the -- where we left off yesterday and then we resumed today, was this whole matter of the Crisis Staffs of the Serbs in the context of Crisis Staffs generally, and that is why, as I said earlier, I would have thought that having regard to the common understanding at which we had arrived earlier, that this is not a matter with which you need tax the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, with all due respect, this witness is, as -- as OTP introduced it, an expert witness on Crisis Staffs. Her theory is that Crisis Staffs of the Bosnian Serbs are the invention of the criminal mind of the Bosnian leadership to create an instrument by which the joint criminal enterprise will be furthered in the territory. That is her assertion. She says, "I couldn't find a single -- a single reference to Crisis Staffs in the -- in the literature," and for this fact she's actually saying that the Crisis Staffs were illegal. I am putting my case to her that she's wrong and that her perception is wrong and that the Crisis Staffs were truly illegal according to the -- to the legal system of -- of the SFRY at the time. And there is nothing criminal about the establishment of these Crisis Staffs if they are established indeed as -- as the committees of -- in accordance with the law. And that is the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, in the interests of time, if in your view this is absolutely necessary, and for myself I'm unpersuaded, please do so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Hanson, I hope I won't be interrupted for a third time by the Prosecution. Would you agree with me that if the Crisis Staffs were conceived on the basis of the law governing total national defence and social self-protection, they were neither illegal nor where they criminal organs. Yes or no? Do you agree with me is what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could explain what you mean by "conceived on the basis"? I see them parallel with these committees, but I do not see a reference to the law itself in the formation of the Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs. And it's not for me to judge whether they're criminal or not. As far as I understand, that's not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, madam. It is my case that they were absolutely based on the law, fully based on the law, and that all those who established them -- well, instead of committees, they would call them Crisis Staffs. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no basis to say they were based on the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Hanson, since you're an historian, I am claiming that this concept of the formation of committees for total national defence and social self-protection only recognises -- is recognised by the legislation of Switzerland, for example, and no other legislation in the world.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that only Swiss legislation has some similar concept, similar to the concept of total -- total national defence and social self-protection?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the legislation of Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with my assertion that the concept stemming from the law on national defence or All People's Defence and social self-protection with respect to the formation of committees under that law never before 1991 on the territory of the former Yugoslavia was used in practice, enforced in practice?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no basis to agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I follow the clock in LiveNote rather than the one on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I follow the clock on LiveNote rather than the one on the wall. It seems that the one on the wall is out by about two minutes so we are just a few seconds short, so if this a convenient point, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just need two minutes at the end of the day if I can raise two issues which would need your attention. Very small, and I think in two minutes we can do it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I recall that Ms. Korner had asked for time at the end of the day as well? No. Okay. Well, we need one minute, so that would be three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Actually, this is the first -- one of the very -- few days that Ms. Korner wasn't asking for the time at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence doesn't have any further questions for this witness. Thank you, Ms. Hanson, very much for your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I say for letting me in the courtroom today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm Igor Pantelic, Defence counsel for Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. Mrs. Hanson, would you take a look on the Exhibit P434, which was marked for identification. Actually, I believe that's your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Test, test, test. Ten, four, ten, four. Is it okay now? I mean, the interpreters will --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Before I pose you certain line of questions and number of questions, please, for the sake of clarity I would very much appreciate your help on -- it's a follow-up issue from -- which was just mentioned by my learned friend Mr. Zecevic with regard to the interpretation in English or the notion of committee for people self-defence and -- the abbreviation which we'll use during this cross-examination will be ONO and DSZ, actually. I will spell, it's Oskar November Oskar, Delta Zulu Sierra [sic]. You maybe can help me because you're an expert in history and these particular categories. Would it be more appropriate, I would say English translation of this abbreviation like ONO means like people -- people's self-protection, All People's Self-Protection, and DSZ is -- well, it's always difficult to translate a certain rough Communist explanations like -- because social, seems to me it's more related to some social welfare or maybe the best way to translate would be a national protection or something like that, DSZ. National self-protection, something to that. What is your opinion about this particular abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opstinado [phoen] Odbrana General -- or All People's Defence, and social self-protection is how I've usually heard it translated. I can't think of a better way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I appreciate it, thank you so much. Mrs. Hanson, so we have on the screen first page of your report, and - sorry - and we could agree, could we not, that this particular -- your report is not related to my client, Mr. Zupljanin, judging from the first page.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't know yet, but I'm speaking about the form. Would you agree with me, would you not, that the first page of your report has nothing to do with my client, Mr. Zupljanin, because this is a report prepared for the case of Mico Stanisic, who is present here, but there is no mention of Zupljanin name, and in addition, our case is IT-08-91-T.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So for the sake of accuracy and for the record, I would kindly ask guidance from the Trial Chamber how we should proceed with this, because potentially this document might become at a certain stage an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Pantelic, if I recall at some point there was a joinder of the cases, so doesn't that answer the question? This report is dated 15 February 2008, which -- and Judge Harhoff would correct me, that was before the joinder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or the arrest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Or the arrest warrant Ms. Korner's at. So is this really in issue, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not for me, Your Honour, but I don't want to split hair into two, but just for the clarity and if the Trial Chamber or, I don't know, the registry, not to mention our friends from the Prosecution side would like to clarify that or if it's a need for that. Otherwise, I'm very relaxed. No problem with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll accept full responsibility for the fact that we omitted to ask Ms. Hanson to amend her report to put on the title page "In the case of Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, it is non-disputed fact that you are an employee of the Office of the Prosecution at ICTY. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how long you are employed by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Up to the present time, I assume.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in your work with the Office of the Prosecution, my understanding that you were mostly focused on certain process of research, analysis, preparing certain memos, drafts for the other members of your team and your office. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a researcher/analyst. That's what I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And at certain stage it's my understanding that actually someone from your office offered you or suggested to you that instead of working on drafting memos, you may be able to produce a report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have certainly continued to draft -- to write memos on various subjects ever -- even since my Crisis Staff memo was first identified as a potential expert report. So it wasn't that I stopped writing memos, it's just that one of my research topics became an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is my understanding -- please, I apologise. It is my understanding that actually you became a sort of by-chance expert within the Office of the Prosecutor, because it was not your original function. It was -- you didn't came here as a -- as an expert from academic circles, but actually it was on the basis of certain needs of your employer. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite my understanding. I came as an expert on the conflict in general. My -- the team I work for, the leadership research team, is people who have some academic background. Obviously I did not arrive as a fully-fledged expert, but it was my own educational background and knowledge that brought me to that team. I worked on a number of topics, one of which, as I said, became identified as a potential expert report. Once the report was named an expert report, I became an expert on that. I had been assigned the topic of Crisis Staffs, but I also work on other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To summarise, Mrs. Hanson, in fact you are in-house expert, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you're not expert in the, I would say, other circles, academics, science or some other circles of -- of activity like -- like university or schools. Not that sort of expert. You are in-house expert for Office of the Prosecution. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am an analyst for the Office of the Prosecution. In my work I have become an expert on this particular topic. As I say, yes, I'm not an expert in science or academics. I'm not sure what you mean by that, but I'm not just an in-house expert is what I'm trying to say. I do other work for the Prosecution besides being the in-house expert on Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I -- my point is -- [Microphone not activated] Sorry. My point is, Mrs. Hanson, in fact you are recognised by your office as an expert, but you are not recognised by the other institutions like academic institutions or, let's say, conferences, various conferences or organisations [indiscernible] for that.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And to -- to go back, to go to the final question of this line, so you would agree with me, would you not, that actually you wrote a report, and then by this act you became an expert for the Prosecution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report, as I said, has been continually updated and I've been working on it, so my expertise does not end with the writing of that first report by a long shot, but, yes, I wrote the report and that made me identified as a potential expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And in your professional background, which personally I must admit it's interesting that you are -- actually, you have a profound knowledge, I would say, about the Russian history and East European history. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My Russian knowledge is only -- it's an undergraduate degree, and then I -- my East European degree was really Balkan history essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I see. Yeah. I mean, when you -- I mean, personally I'm interested because being a semi-Russian, you know, I'd just like to find some connections. But Kennan Institute for advanced Russian studies, it was in DC you say.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you say you were -- after your college you were performing certain researches. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And tell me, probably you were travel around. I mean, Central Europe or Russia or Balkans, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What's your --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mostly where? In which region? I assume Bosnia, but apart of Bosnia -- aside of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relevant to my work here, the entire former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you were in -- I mean, correct me. It's my impression with your -- also you were -- you are winner of Fulbright scholarship.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You might be an excellent person with an exquisite profile for American intelligence services especially in this period when you are travelling around Balkans. Am I right with my impression? I mean, because you have certain experience from Ivy League. You know, it's a very -- very high-ranked universities. I mean, would you say that you might be interested for intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I would be interested?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, they for you.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had no contact with them so reason to think they are interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you are now telling us for the record that you were never approached by any member of American or other foreign intelligence services from the period of 1984 up to now, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly never to my knowledge approached by anyone from American services. I lived in Belgrade, worked at the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. I had a few peculiar, you know, encounters one has. I can't say. I was not aware that I was approached by any foreign intelligence service, but I imagine I was of interest to them because I was, as you say, an interesting-looking person working in the JNA General Staff. So I cannot say that no one that I talked to was not from the Serbian or Yugoslav intelligence services, but I certainly had never any reason to think -- to say that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During -- because, you know, Mrs. Hanson, this is a very interesting period when you were in Belgrade. It was from -- I take it from your CV it's from 1990 until 1992. It's the break-up of Yugoslavia, lots of -- I mean, it's very -- it's a coincidence you were there --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I take it that absolutely you don't have, but tell me, at that time do you remember who was ambassador for US in Belgrade in period of 1990 until 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Warren Zimmermann that I remember. I don't remember if there were others, some changeover at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you in situation to meet personally Mr. Zimmermann in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a Fulbright scholar, yes. There was some Fulbright party that he was at, and I think I went to the US Embassy 4th of July party, but that was the extent of my contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Once, twice, dozens?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice. Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Aside of Ambassador Zimmermann with some other employees or functionaries from American Embassy, did you -- because finally I mean you were living there for two years, I mean in this very, I would say, tension period. You know, the old guy Milosevic in power with all his stuff that he's doing. So for one American, it will be a little bit uncomfortable to be there. So you were in contact on a regular basis, I believe, with your society from the embassy or some other Americans at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a Fulbright scholar, yes, I had contact in the embassy because the scholarship programme was overseen by the embassy or -- I can't remember the exact form of the contact, but, yes, and I would go to the American club which is located on the embassy premises, not once a week but maybe once a month, would buy things at the shop there, but it was purely social. I never -- there was one woman who was in charge of -- I forget the name of the programme but the part of Department of State concerning cultural affairs. She was my contact. I took her once to the General Staff to meet some of the people at the institute, but that was just a formal diplomatic sort of meet and greet, but I never had any -- any work-related contact with them. It was just social.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I remember good barbecue and beers in American club in embassy. I share your opinion. But tell me, Mrs. Hanson, did you travel at that time from Serbia to Bosnia? Did you visit Bosnia at this period of time between 1990 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where? Where have you been?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo and Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly a few words explain what was the purpose of your trip to Sarajevo and Zvornik area at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo I was -- a friend of mine was visiting. He's a Norwegian diplomat, and he wanted to -- he was just meeting various people, sort of -- so I introduced him to a couple of people in Belgrade and then he wanted to see Sarajevo. So we went there. The Zvornik area is -- it was personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And tell me, at this period of time what was your area of research in -- in -- correct me if I'm wrong, in -- I can give you a name of the institution. Military Historical Institute of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was researching my dissertation topic for my Ph.D., which was on the army of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, the inter-war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And after this period being in Serbia, you left to the States, I believe, or after 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May of 1992 I left Belgrade and returned to the States. I stopped in Norway to see those friends, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I take it that during your visit to Bosnia it was the outbreak of hostilities there or it was still calm, because --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 1st of April, 1992, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 1st of April, 1992, and you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Apart of being in-house expert, maybe somebody will call you for a witness, you know, viva voce because you're a fact witness too. But tell me, how long you were there in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I believe it was just two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah. And between 1992 and 1999, have you often visited region of Bosnia-Herzegovina? For of course your research and --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one time, between -- yeah, between 1992 and starting here in 1999 only one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't for research. It was for something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So when you came here, you start your work as a political analyst, among other fields of activity in -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the main topic, I would say, or -- or area, and I believe it still is now, research on top political leadership of Republika Srpska. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team as a whole deals with the political leadership. At first -- the first two years I was not on Republika Srpska. I was on FRY, Federal Yugoslavia -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And during your work, it's undisputed fact that you were able to read and analyse tons, I would say, materials, pages, thousands pages.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what is your personal opinion after reading all these pages? What is your personal opinion about the SDS party? Do you like SDS party? What is your opinion? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- simple --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is different from my professional. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you like or dislike SDS? Simple question. Simple answer.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't care. I don't have feelings of like or dislike for it. It's a topic I studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you are neutral to SDS, SDS policy, SDS programme, statute. That's simple question. Give me a simple --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly neutral to the statute of the party, and I consider it my job to be as neutral as possible in everything I look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But what about Dr. Radovan Karadzic? What -- do you like him or dislike him? What is your personal position? No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it has gone on for a while but I think it's about time I stood up now and noted my objection to his questions about her personal opinion on these different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I declined to intervene waiting on the cue from the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Where are we going?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are going, Your Honour, to establish the personal approach of this witness with regard to certain institutions, certain personalities. We are going, Your Honour, to the road of objectivity or to the road of bias. So I want to establish Mrs. Hanson personal approach to this very matters. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I anticipated that reply, Mr. Pantelic, but it seems that it's possible for you to lay this foundation for your challenge of bias much more succinctly than you've been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Hanson, being an employee of the Office of the Prosecution, you are actually an important part of the team to assist and to prove Prosecution theory of the case. I'm speaking about this particular case, Stanisic and Zupljanin. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my job to prove their theory. It's my job to give them the facts that I have found, the evidence I have found. And I do not serve them if I present a biased view. I do not serve them if I do not give them the whole truth. I understand that to be my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You'd agree with me, would you not, that this is a rather unique and, I would say, almost impossible position. How you can be neutral and stand on the objective level but at the same time working for the Office of the Prosecution, being paid by the Office of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- I must shut down from that line because she having been -- this matter has been dealt with in the Appeals Chamber and she's been deemed an expert in this trial. So that line is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely I will follow your direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mrs. Hanson, maybe I will be back on certain aspects of this issue, but of course under the instruction of the Trial Chamber and following the direction. Tell me, Mrs. Hanson, you are not an expert in constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are not an expert in public international law.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are not an expert in police matters.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you assume yourself as an expert for political issues. Am I correct? Speaking of -- sorry. Before you answer, speaking about the political aspects, events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, 1992, and this period. How -- how you will describe your credentials regarding that issue?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My credentials, as I have said before, my educational background as an historian, my experience as an analyst, my knowledge from the documents I've read. Yes, I have a knowledge about the events in the former Yugoslavia that certainly far exceeds the average person's. I've been identified as an expert on this topic of crisis staffs --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Hanson. It's a very simple question. Are you considering yourself as a political expert -- expert, sorry, for the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina? More directly and more specifically, I'm asking you are you familiar with the events before the proclamation of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Are you familiar with the political life, political players in that region and the, let's say, period after the beginning of 1992 in terms of political development? Simply as that. Are you consider yourself familiar to be an expert?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there's a large --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes or no [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- between -- familiar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But not as -- you're not an expert in political life in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm too modest to call myself an expert but I'll say I'm familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. My learned friend Mr. Zecevic covered practically almost all areas and aspects, so I would like to summarise for the sake of the transcript and for the sake of this case. First of all, would you agree with me, would you not, Mrs. Hanson, that Bosnia-Herzegovina was comparing to the other former Yugoslav republic specific in terms of the existence of three constituent nations at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that certain safeguards or let me say some constitutional or political mechanism were imposed to protect the sort of vital interest of all three constituent nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time period are you talking about, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three nations were recognised in the constitution, but I can't speak with certainty of the constitutional mechanisms imposed, as you say, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So if I tell you that the certain principles of protection of vital interest of each nation existed at that time, do you have any reason to doubt my proposition?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I'm familiar with the principle. I'm not familiar with the mechanism that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how would you described being person familiar with the political issues? With respect I would say, how would you describe the development in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the mid of October 1991, which eventually resulted in -- in organisation of Serbian plebiscite? How would you describe this events in short words?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Slovenia and Croatia were leaving the former Yugoslavia, the issue then of the status of Bosnia arose. The Serb side was eager to keep Bosnia within a reduced Yugoslavia. The other national parties were figuring out how best to protect their interests and whether to secure -- to see if Bosnia should go the route of independence. The future was uncertain. Things were tense. I'm sorry, I'm not very good at a history lecture off the top of my head. I don't know what more --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I agree. I agree. I will try to help you and to refresh your memory and to try to go together through this line of questioning. I agree. Let me remind you that on the -- in the mid of October, Serbian deputies were over-voted in Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they left this. Are you familiar with this fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wonder how this ties into Ms. Hanson's testimony. The scope of her expertise is very clear, Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs. I'm just not sure how this fits in and how she is an expert to be answering these questions at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, my dear friend, Mrs. Hanson -- my understanding is that -- and, Your Honour, she is the -- among all other areas, I try to find and I think I found that she's more familiar with the political issues than all other issues that -- including the other issues that she's speaking. So I try to -- with her to go to the conclusion and the origins of the formation of Crisis Staff and the function of the Crisis Staff, but starting from certain point, because it's fact of common knowledge here that Crisis Staff didn't land from the Mars in Bosnia. So let's see the background of certain events which led to the ultimate issue, which is the case here, and that's why Mrs. Hanson is testifying. So I think it's perfectly legitimate question, especially because she's political analyst, Your Honour. But she is not police expert. She is not lawyer. She is not public international lawyer. So what shall I ask her apart of this? That's my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think we understand that, Mr. Pantelic, and of course we know that everything has a prior cause, but we needn't go all the way back to the garden of Eden. So if you could bring it nearer home to the expertise which this witness -- on the basis of which this witness was proffered by the Prosecution it would be in everybody's interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, that's my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So when the Serbian deputies were over-voted and by the way, being a political analyst you can agree with me that many authors, very serious authors, wrote about, like Susan Woodward, you are familiar with her, like I think Robert Biden or even Ambassador Zimmermann wrote about all these events, so you would agree with me that the turning point, the milestone for the later events in Bosnia were the moment of over-voting of Serbian deputies in Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I right? Just speaking about this moment.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing is inevitable. Decisions were made throughout, so I wouldn't say there's one turning point. People always had choices on how to act. So I wouldn't say that one event meant that all the later events were absolutely inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But finally, I mean, this particular event happened. Am I right? Where the Serbs were over-voted in Bosnia Assembly and left the Assembly. Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't like -- sorry. I don't want to hear, sorry, Mrs. Hanson, because you want to go faster. It's not a matter of your opinion. You will have opportunity to express your opinion when my learned friend will ask you in re-examination. It's a simple fact. You're political analyst. You're drafting and submitting your report. My simple question is: Are you aware that in the mid of October, between 14 and 15 of October, Serbian deputies left Bosnian Assembly due to the over-voting by Muslim and Croat deputies? Yes or no? Are you familiar or are you not familiar? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let's go to another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I must say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- this witness may be an expert in the history of the former Republic of Yugoslavia and in many other issues, but she is called here as an expert in relation to the Serbian Crisis Staffs, and I think you have to stick to that particular area and to stay there, actually. So this may all be very interesting, but this witness is not here to testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely agree with you. What I needed it's only one simple yes and then I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, because you keep pursuing the benefit of this witness's particular knowledge about the history of the affairs, but as interesting as that might be, it is beyond the scope of her expertise for these purposes as a witness in this trial. You have to stay very close to the area of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then I'm sure you are familiar with the fact that these Serbian MPs or deputies, they formed a Serbian Assembly, actually Assembly of Serbian nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina after they left Bosnian-Herzegovinian Assembly. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And tell me, are you aware, because you read a lot of documents, from which parties were Serbian MPs in this particular Assembly, Serbian Assembly? Can you give us a list if you know?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority were from the SDS. There were some from the SPO, maybe one of the reform -- the Union of Reformist Forces. I can't be sure, but certainly the great majority was SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how many deputies were Serbian Assembly consist of?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in the -- many cases -- no, no. I will come to that later. Sorry. After the formation of Assembly of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they in January, I believe, proclaimed Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but let's call it Republika Srpska. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What's the use of agreeing with Judge Harhoff, Judge Harhoff's remark, and then continue as if nothing were? I mean, what -- what's the relation to the topic of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I will just come to that point immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Hanson, tell me, are you familiar with the fact that after the formation of Republika Srpska a process of -- of formation of Serbian municipality actually took place in the beginning of 1992? Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them took place before that. Already in November the Assembly is calling for Serbian Municipal Assemblies and Serbian municipalities. The formation started, we see, late December in some places. So from late -- from December on, I would say, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us, please, these Serbian municipalities were consist of which parties, deputies? Can you tell us? To be honest with you, would you agree with me that actually the structure of -- of Serbian MPs in -- in Assembly of Serbia -- Serbian Republic actually mirrored on a municipal level more or less?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most municipalities, yes. Most Serbs voted for the SDS. Not every municipality, but most of them. So when the Serb deputies left Municipal Assemblies and formed Serbian Municipal Assemblies, they were largely SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it was perfectly legitimate, I would say in political terms, fact that if SDS won elections in Bosnia, practically they were on the basis of this result in majority also in Municipal Assemblies. Am I right? I mean, the point is, they are not came there like invaders. I mean, they were elected.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were elected in municipal elections to the Municipal Assemblies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sure. And tell me, are you aware of the fact that -- for example, how familiar are you with the Crisis Staff issue and the development in -- in Samac municipality? Did you -- were you able to -- to perform certain research on that municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read documents of the Samac Crisis Staff. I didn't prepare it per se. I have read many documents, and therefore although I'm familiar in general terms, without consulting the documents again I wouldn't want to speak with any authority, but I've certainly read the documents of the Samac Crisis Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And fortunately I was -- I was a Defence counsel for a mayor of Samac and the chief of Crisis Staffs so I'm a little bit more familiar, of course we have a final judgement in that case. Are you aware of the fact that in Samac Crisis Staff other political parties were -- I mean, the members of other political parties were a member of that Crisis Staff? Are you aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- Mr. Zecevic also earlier asked me about that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar that, for example, a former Communist Party SDP member was -- was at the same time member of Samac municipality? Just tell me. If you don't remember, I take it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I don't contest it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that a member of social democratic party was -- was actually a member of Samac municipality Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isn't that the SDP?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was -- actually -- sorry, it was Ante Markovic reformist, Reformist Party. Sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not specifically aware of that, of the membership, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also you're aware and you confirm that member of Muslim people, Muslim community, was at the same time member of Samac Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the name. The name, of course, suggests Muslim. I'm not aware of his party affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of the fact that for example in a certain number of -- of municipalities like -- like Samac, like Sanski Most, like Doboj, among all three parties, meaning Serb, Croat, and Muslim, through their Crisis Staff in the beginning of 1992, more precisely in March and April, there were ongoing discussions and negotiations with regard to the -- to the formation of -- of various municipalities along the lines of -- of national parties? Are you aware of the fact that members of SDA, HDZ, and SDS negotiated in terms of splitting municipality territory in this couple of examples? Are you aware about the fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of in Samac, not Doboj and Sanski Most, but I have seen it also in other municipalities this topic raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the -- my point, actually. So you -- I don't think you have a reason to -- to disagree with me, but you take it as a normal political process of negotiation among the parties in light of the local and municipal interest. I mean, nothing -- nothing illegitimate in this process. How do you find this?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not find it a normal political process both from the documents I've seen and what witnesses I know have said, but the process of dividing the municipalities was not accepted on all sides, was not seen as legitimate on all sides, and was not -- it was not a free and relaxed negotiation by -- by any means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: By being -- by being political analyst and researcher, you are aware that number of international efforts and mediations were put on the scene at the beginning of 1992 in order to find a solution to resolve the crisis in Bosnia. Are you aware about that, about international efforts?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that, for example, on the basis of Lisbon conference, we call it Cutileiro Plan, the general framework for the constitutional, I would say basis for Bosnia-Herzegovina future were adopted. Are you aware of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Whereas three constituent nation in Bosnia practically were, I would say, advised to form three entities within Bosnia. Are you aware about it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of that same plan, certain territory of a number of municipalities simply were divided. Are you aware about that aspect of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cutileiro --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just yes or no. Don't -- because let's go to other topic. Are you aware or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the situation based on Dayton Peace Accord where a certain number of municipalities actually were split on the basis of that agreement? Are you aware about that fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in conclusion, are you ready to reconsider your previous answer with regard to the process of formation of new municipalities based on what you just gave me answers?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is your right, by all means. And tell me, what do you know about the region called Autonomous Region of Krajina? Abbreviation is ARK. What is your personal knowledge of that entity?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the general steps in its formation. I am aware -- I've seen many documents from it. There's been a whole case --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about it. If you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I can be. Let's start from the beginning. Tell me when this ARK region was formed. According to your knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was -- that term was given to the earlier community of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina in, I would say, August 1991, but I'm not quite sure. That's not what I prepared for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's no problem. I will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I call, please -- it's 65 ter document number 17. Actually, this is the statute of ARK. So we could take a look and make some -- some questions here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So could you -- okay. Good. What we have on the -- on the bottom left side is "September 1991." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have the second page, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the preamble of this document we have an exact date. This is the 16 of September, 1991. You -- you see that. Also, we see the legal basis for the formation of that region. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To be precise, the basis was the certain provisions of constitution of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So now, actually, we are speaking of the certain constitutional form of the region. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they cite, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then in your work analysing the decisions and activities of -- of ARK, could you tell us, please, who were the members of Assembly of ARK at that time? I mean, in terms of party or ...

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is the Assembly would be made up majority of SDS representatives, but I have not looked at that part of ARK in any depth, and I'm reluctant to talk much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I can help you maybe. SDA also members were there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps if we could see the document that this information is coming from rather than perhaps testing the -- Ms. Hanson's memory. It may help us move through this quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It will be almost impossible, Your Honour, because informations are coming from my head. So it will be very painful for me to cut the -- to cut the -- this part of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. But could we agree that on the basis of multi-party elections in 1990 all practically parties, including SDS, SDA, HDZ and Reformist were actually members of Assembly of ARK? Say yes, if you know. Say no if you don't know. Simply as that.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with that statement, because the -- there were no elections to the Assembly of ARK in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, to that extent you're right, but what was the basis of formation of ARK?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on an earlier form of association of municipalities which did exist on, as far as I understood, of economic interest, the association of municipality of Bosanska Krajina was the basis for the formation of ARK, but it was a big step from association of municipalities to autonomous region, and although the various municipalities might have sent deputies from different parties to the association of municipalities, by the time it became this autonomous region it became a largely Serbian and SDS endeavour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but can you tell me, you would agree with me that in ARK the Assembly was formed actually, at that time.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of ARK --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was formed. I don't know enough about the mechanisms of the association of municipalities to know if there was an Assembly of that. Again, it's not a topic that I claim to be an expert on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. My question was simply because you mentioned that you personally went through all this documents, all the mechanism. That's why I'm asking you this several questions, because in fact my point is that before the formation of -- of Republika Srpska, on the basis of constitutional principles and provisions of socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina actually ARK was formed. And in the Assembly of ARK were on the basis of certain results of election all three nations. That's my point. Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is there were no elections to the Assembly of ARK, so I can't answer that. And the constitutional provisions for the association of municipalities does not provide for the kind of powers that ARK gave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with your -- with your information, but let's go to page 8 of B/C/S version, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may interrupt just to allow for the possibility of Mr. Zecevic's two minutes and the Chamber's one minute exceeding 180 seconds, perhaps you could wind down now to allow us time to deal with those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. By all means. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's go to -- to Article 28 of -- of the statute of ARK where we see that we have -- yes, sorry. 28, yes. Where we see the organs of the Assembly, which is of course chairman or speaker, vice-president, second vice-president, and the provisions that the method of the election shall be -- shall be determined by the Assembly, and they were all member -- they were all member of the Assembly. And actually, this was based and formed on the basis of elections from 1991. In fact, Mrs. Hanson, are you aware of the fact that the Assembly of ARK was formed and where all political parties and representatives of all three nations were work on the basis of the provisions of this statute? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then can you take a look on the Article 41 of the statute where -- 41, yes. This is page 11 of -- yeah. Could you -- could you just scroll up, please, this page. Okay. So we see in article 41 that this statute actually is the -- replacing a previous statute of self-governing regional community of Banja Luka municipality with regard to the provisions of Official Gazette number 11 from 77, which means that actually this region was even established almost 20 years ago. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I already talked about the association of municipalities. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that ARK was actually successor of this previous body. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It declared itself to be the successor, yes, but it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But on the basis -- Mrs. Hanson, please, not on the basis of Serbian constitution but on the basis of Bosnian and Herzegovinian constitution. Don't forget we passed this issue in the preamble. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. They cited the constitution. I don't know that specific provision that they cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I think it's now time for this couple of hundreds of seconds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Hanson, you'll appreciate that your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You will appreciate your testimony is not yet at an end. We will resume tomorrow morning in Courtroom I at 9.00, and I will now ask the usher to escort you from the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In its assessment of the Rule 92 bis evidence, the Trial Chamber noticed that in relation to Witness ST-48, the Prosecution seeks to tender one statement given by the witness on 10 March 2003 to the Prosecution's investigators. However, while this statement is provided in B/C/S, no English translation can be found in the Rule 92 bis package provided. Moreover, the electronic file for Witness ST-48 contains the following two additional statements that are not listed either in Annex A or Annex B to the motion: One, one statement given by the witness to Prosecution's investigators on 8 December 1989, which is provided in B/C/S and English and two, one statement given by the witness to the Bavarian Criminal Investigations Department in Munich on 17 November 1998, which is provided in B/C/S, English, and German. For these reasons the Trial Chamber orders the Prosecution to submit the English translation of the 10th of March 2003 statement as soon as possible before the recess and to clarify if it seeks to tender into evidence the above-mentioned two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't the faintest idea who Witness ST-48 is, but do you want a motion filed again or simply could we just hand over the translation if we haven't already done it and whatever else it is you are requiring? All you want to do is put it in e-court. You don't want us to file a motion. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honours. Your Honours, there are two or three issues very shortly. We have here in The Hague our joint expert and police professor Bajagic, and with the leave of the Trial Chamber, we would like to have him during the examination of the next witness, Mr. Nielsen, to have him at -- at our hand, so to speak, inside the courtroom to follow the testimony of the expert witness which he will be confronting in his testimony during the Defence case. Now, this is -- Mr. Bajagic is our joint expert for Zupljanin and Stanisic team. He will -- he is nominated. He is appointed as our expert, and he will appear in our Defence team -- in our Defence case. I'm sorry. I'm a bit tired. So we will want the Trial Chamber is a leave that he is present here in the courtroom during the testimony of expert Mr. Nielsen, that he can advise us and give us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's see if the Prosecution has a view on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. The second thing, Your Honours, I would kindly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Zecevic, did I hear you correctly that this person who you would wish to have -- whose assistance you would wish to have immediately would later be called as a witness by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he is an expert, there is no objection to it indeed. I mean, in many jurisdictions now there would be a full exchange of experts reports. If he is being called as an expert and only as an expert and not as a witness as to fact, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Only as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees. The second matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The second matter, Your Honours, is we will ask kindly the leave of the Trial Chamber for the cross-examination of Mr. Nielsen that both counsels can deal with the cross-examination, because, Your Honours, Mr. Nielsen initially was my witness but due to the schedule I couldn't prepare Mr. -- Ms. Hanson and Mr. Nielsen parallelly. So therefore Mr. Cvijetic will conduct the first part of the cross-examination and then I will, with your leave, continue cross-examining the witness Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There's no difficulty with your sharing the work if that's how --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the third thing, Your Honours, we discussed the -- our filing for the documents with -- with Ms. Hanson, and I would just like an indication when does the Trial Chamber expects us to file that motion with the documents, for admission of the documents in two groups?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we answer that tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means you can, Your Honour. I was just hoping that I -- that my time doesn't run out tomorrow. That's why I'm bringing it up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, needless to say I am reminded of something I do want to raise. It will take 30 seconds. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, private session.
